new.n: Peerless logging railroad piling at the Fish Creek mouth (1890s)
new.pl: Mouth of Fish Creek, west end of Chequamegon Bay, Ashland
new.v: Piling stubs, trestle footings, spikes and tie plates
new.st: Peerless logging railroad (mid-1890s), Ashland-Bayfield counties. Built by Ashland West End millmen with $65,000 of County Board help (about $120,000 spent in all) to haul logs from the Moquah country to the DSS&A. Ran 25 miles: from the foot of the Blast Furnace bluff along the shore to near the mouth of Fish Creek, where piling carried a wooden roadbed over the water; near Whittlesey Creek it ran parallel to Cherryville Road and crossed gullies and ravines on stilts; at Moquah it turned south to a junction with the South Shore at Bibon. 'Soon became a memory only.'. Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Piling stubs in the bay shallows, trestle footings in the gullies, spikes and tie plates on the grade.
pinev: Pin at the Fish Creek mouth, where the book puts the over-water piling; good to about 500 m. The grade ran from there along Cherryville Rd and south from Moquah to Bibon.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Cook's (later Smeaton's) sawmill near Prentice Park, Ashland
new.pl: Shore near Prentice Park, west end of Ashland
new.v: Slab fill and mill iron along the shore
new.st: Cook's sawmill, later Smeaton's, near Prentice Park, Ashland West End. Took the Peerless railroad's logs; destroyed by fire. Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Waterfront slab fill, mill-site iron along the shore near the park.
pinev: Pin on the shore by Prentice Park; the book says only "near Prentice Park", so good to about 500 m.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: George Stuntz's fur post near Bay City Creek, Ashland (1850s)
new.st: George R. Stuntz's Chequamegon Bay fur post, 'near Bay City Creek', Ashland (1850s; Stuntz later Duluth's first permanent settler and Vermilion Range discoverer). Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Trade silver, beads, gunflints; inside city limits, permission needed.
pinev: Pin at the Bay City Creek mouth (Overture water); the book says "near Bay City Creek", so good to about 500 m. The Bay City townsite pin (ob-bay-city-ashland) is 2 km west.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Houghton Point brownstone quarry and the stranded 1893 monolith
new.pl: Houghton Point, west shore of Chequamegon Bay NE of Washburn
new.st: Houghton Point brownstone quarry and the 1893 monolith, Bayfield Co. (between Washburn and Ashland on the W shore of the bay). In 1890-93 quarrymen cut a tapered monolith 110 ft long, 10 ft square at the base and 4 ft at the top for the Chicago world's fair; the Panic of '93 stranded it 'in its bed' for several years before it was cut into building blocks. The 'old village site' of Houghton is about a mile away, near the quarry (fisherman Nels Bodin's best catches). Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Quarry camp and village site; drill steel, wedges, camp coins.
src: Harris, Chequamegon Country 1659-1976 (1976), p 370 (shot 232L) and p 205 (shot 205R area)
pinev: Pin at the end of the Houghton Point roads on the point; the quarry face is not placed, so good to about 500 m.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Nourse brothers' sugar bush, SW of Bayfield (1850s-60s)
new.pl: About 3 mi SW of Bayfield, 4 mi W of Pikes Bay
new.v: Sugar-camp kettle sites, spiles, trade items
new.st: Nourse brothers' sugar bush, Bayfield Co.: an 80-acre maple grove 4 mi W of Pike's Bay and 3 mi SW of Bayfield, 'Wisconsin's oldest sugar bush' area; early settlers' mecca, up to 1,900 sap pails and 300 gallons of syrup a spring (1850s-60s; Rev. Peet's diary). Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Sugar-camp kettle sites, spiles, trade items.
pinev: Placed from the book's distances only (3 mi SW of Bayfield, 4 mi W of Pikes Bay); good to about 2 km. Check the 1880s plat for a Nourse forty.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Aksel Holter's 1907 ski slide at the White River bridge, S of Ashland
new.pl: Wisconsin Central (Soo Line) crossing of the White River, south of Ashland
new.v: Coins and tokens dropped by a 5,000-person crowd
new.st: Aksel Holter's 1907 ski slide near the Wisconsin Central's White River bridge, S of Ashland: one Sunday 5,000 or more people watched 'the country's best jumpers' (first big ski meet in the area). Unconfirmed, one source.
new.t: Crowds of 5,000 drop coins; spectator slope at the foot of the jump.
src: Harris, Chequamegon Country 1659-1976 (1976), p 279 area (Holter, chap. XLVIII)
pinev: Pin at the Wisconsin Central crossing of the White River (Overture rail and water lines meet here); the slide was "near" the bridge, so good to about 500 m.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.pl: Drummond Lake shore by the village, Bayfield Co.
new.st: Drummond's big Rust-Owen Lumber Co. mill, Bayfield Co., on the Omaha railroad 33 mi SW of Ashland. Rust-Owen owned about four-fifths of the timber in four townships; logs came by rail and stream. 'When the big Drummond mill was only a memory, the village was showing its ghostly look.' The 1894 fire also burned Drummond, Cable, Mason and Benoit. Unconfirmed, one source.
src: Harris, Chequamegon Country 1659-1976 (1976), p 207 area (shot 138R); fire p 216 area
pinev: Pin on the south shore of Drummond Lake by the village; the mill footprint is not placed yet, so good to about 500 m.
Unconfirmed, one source

new.n: Camp Stella and the West Bay Club, Sand Island
new.pl: West Bay, Sand Island, Apostle Islands
new.st: Camp Stella / West Bay Club, Sand Island (Apostle Islands). Sam Fifield's Camp Stella (with his little steamer Stella) on West Bay; later bought by a St. Paul group, the West Bay Club (Frank Ehas), who built a dock costing about $5,000 and a grocery store. Frank Shaw's small fishery was in the East Bay area. Howard (Bud) Peters, Mellen mayor, later logged his third of the island. Unconfirmed, one source.
src: Harris, Chequamegon Country 1659-1976 (1976), pp 199, 368, 376; Ashland Daily Press 30 Jul 1948 (cited)
pinev: Pin in the West Bay area of Sand Island; good to about 1 km.
Unconfirmed, one source
acc: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore: look only

new.st: Vernie Butler's year-round hermitage, Rocky Island (Apostle Islands), mid-1900s: lived alone through winters, came to Bayfield each November on herring boats for shells, batteries and supplies; earlier camp on the Sioux River near Washburn and a winter hideout near Cornucopia. National Lakeshore: LOOK-ONLY. Layer: history. Tier C. Unconfirmed, one source.

t-hermit-island.st: Harris (1976, ch. XXXIX 'Hermit Wilson's fallacy of hidden treasure') calls the gold a myth: William Wilson built his log cabin in Oct 1847 (dock, cobblestone-and-mud chimney); Ben Armstrong had earlier counted his coin bags at about $1,300; after the Oct 1861 murder the bags were gone and only $60 was found behind a clock. Excursion captain Bob Weber of the Chippewa spread the 'big treasure of gold' tale to thousands of tourists. Keep 'legend'; consider moving the $91,000 figure to 'later retellings'.

wk-fedora.st: Harris (1976): a lamp exploded in the engine room in Sept 1901 and fire spread before anyone could slow the ship, which ran onto the rocks off Basswood ('Bass') Island; she was 55 years old, Duluth-bound out of Hancock.

ob-bay-city-ashland.st: Harris (1976): after the 1857 panic and Civil War talk every family but Martin Roehm's left; 'empty were fifty houses of log and frame', and no Ashlander served in the Union Army because the village was deserted. Roehm ran cattle on the Marengo River and drove them to Odanah, the Bad River mouth and Chequamegon Point. In 1920 the wooden bridge over Bay City Creek was 'unsafe for motor trucks'; nearby were Poziski's big junk yard and the abandoned Keystone horse barns.

rr-hotel-chequamegon.st: Harris (1976): old Farragut sailor Judd ran passengers from the Chequamegon Hotel dock to stops on the Apostle Islands.

it-tanner-forty-sec26.st: On the Ashland druggist who bought the Chief's silver: Harris (1976) gives H. D. Weed, New York-born, 33 in 1872, trained in his uncle's Ithaca drugstore, went to California via Panama in 1850 and made $5,000 mining in a year, then ran drugstores in Milwaukee and Chicago before Ashland. So the buyer knew ore. Harris says nothing about the silver itself.
src: Harris, Chequamegon Country 1659-1976 (1976), p 140 area (Ashland 1872 roster)

tg-radisson-fort-ashland.st: Harris (1976) agrees: Allouez's 1665 bark chapel, Wisconsin's first church, stood near the head of Chequamegon Bay, not on Madeline Island.

mf-frenchtown.st: Two independent papers add to this. The 13 June 1880 flood, 23 ft above the high-water mark, ran eight feet over Frenchtown, "a half a mile below the city, and which has stood for the last thirty years", and completely covered a few small houses (Chippewa Times, reprinted in the Eau Claire News, 19 Jun 1880, p. 2). A 1912 retrospective puts Frenchtown "on the south side of the Chippewa river, about opposite the Furniture factory". It adds that it was long a question "whether Frenchtown or Chippewa Falls would be the city" (Chippewa Independent, reprinted in the Eau Claire Leader-Telegram, 1 Dec 1912, p. 2). So the ground was buried by flood sand in 1880 and swept again in 1884.
src: Eau Claire News, 19 Jun 1880, p. 2, "The Flood at the Falls" (from the Chippewa Times)
Eau Claire Leader-Telegram, 1 Dec 1912, p. 2 (from the Chippewa Independent)
